leads.name: Steel's Tavern Oaks
leads.species: Live Oak (Quercus virginiana or Quercus fusiformis, not yet settled)
leads.reason: Three live oaks on the bluff 50 yards northwest of the Tarrant County Courthouse, the only living things left from the 1849 army post that gave Fort Worth its name; they also mark the site of Steel's Tavern, the town's first hotel and stagecoach stop from 1855. A county historical marker stands with them. Ensemble of three at one standing point, so it plausibly passes the collectible-point test. Public ground downtown.

location.address: 200 West Bluff Street, Fort Worth, TX

leads.name: Traders Oak
leads.reason: The live oak behind which traders Daggett and Leonard built their log store in 1849, a mile from the fort because army rules kept merchants that far off; it became the area's first lasting business, trading with Native visitors camped at the spring nearby. It now has a small city park named after it. Species as given by the finding aid, to be confirmed.

leads.name: Turner Oak
leads.species: Live Oak (Quercus virginiana or Quercus fusiformis, not yet settled)
leads.reason: Pioneer Charles Turner, who opposed secession but refused to swap his savings for Confederate paper, buried his gold under this oak on his 1851 farm and dug it up after the Civil War to help the young town pay its debts. The farm is now Greenwood Memorial Park cemetery. Needs: a recent alive confirmation and the spot inside the cemetery; access line should state cemetery hours.

location.address: Greenwood Memorial Park, Fort Worth, TX

blocked.name: Parker Oaks

location.address: Post Oak-Parker Cemetery, 1301 Cardinal Lane, Hurst, TX 76053

blocked.why_blocked: NOT A COLLECTIBLE POINT (2026-09-27 verify pass). The cemetery is genuinely public (a City of Hurst park, officially named Post Oak-Parker Cemetery, designated a Historic Texas Cemetery in 2020, 1301 Cardinal Lane) and Isaac Duke Parker's biography checks out against TSHA, but the trees themselves are, in the nursery's own words, "this stand of large post oaks" surrounding the cemetery, and the city's own page calls it "a good stand of trees, many of which are post oaks." Two historical markers on site (1968 "Parker Cemetery" and 1984 "I.D. Parker Public Cemetery") commemorate the CEMETERY, not any individual tree, and no source names, numbers or marks one specific specimen Cynthia Ann Parker is said to have sat beneath. A grove around a 2.4-acre cemetery with no single obvious place to stand fails the one-collectible-point rule (an avenue or a whole wood is blocked). Would need a source naming one specific tree (a plaque, a marker, a documented single specimen) to ever qualify; absent that it stays blocked rather than a lead, since the ensemble itself does not read as a compact, single-destination point.
